readings.title: First reading
readings.text:
Woe to those who plot evil,
who lie in bed planning mischief!
No sooner is it dawn than they do it
– their hands have the strength for it.
Seizing the fields that they covet,
they take over houses as well,
owner and house they confiscate together,
taking both man and inheritance.
So the Lord says this:
Now it is I who plot
such mischief against this breed
as your necks will not escape;
nor will you be able to walk proudly,
so evil will the time be.
On that day they will make a satire on you,
sing a dirge and say,
‘We are stripped of everything;
my people’s portion is measured out and shared,
no one will give it back to them,
our fields are awarded to our despoiler.’
Therefore you will have no one
to measure out a share
in the community of the Lord.

exegesis.summary: Micah pronounces woe upon those who lie awake scheming how to seize the fields and houses of the poor, using the power of their hands to devour the inheritance of others. The Lord answers their plotting with His own: He will measure out judgment against them, so that they who took shares from the helpless will themselves have no share in the assembly of the Lord. It is a stern reminder that God sees every hidden injustice and defends the inheritance of the little ones.

patristicQuotes.quote: We are placed in this life not as lords in our own house, but as guests and strangers. Know thyself to be a dispenser of the things of others, and that the privileges granted thee are for a brief and passing use. Cast away then from thy soul the pride of power, and put on the humility and modesty of a steward.

Tell me what is thine, from whence didst thou get it and bring it into life? If every one receiving what is sufficient for his own necessity would leave what remains to the needy, there would be no rich or poor.

cccReferences.title: Love for the poor incompatible with selfish riches
Old Testament measures for the poor

exegesis.thematicConnection: Micah gives voice to the very oppression the Psalm laments and identifies the wicked whom Christ, the gentle Servant of the Gospel, comes to unmask and to overthrow — not by their violence, but by His meekness that will not break the crushed reed.

readings.title: Responsorial Psalm
readings.text:
Lord, do not forget the poor.
Lord, why do you stand afar off
and hide yourself in times of distress?
The poor man is devoured by the pride of the wicked:
he is caught in the schemes that others have made.
Lord, do not forget the poor.
For the wicked man boasts of his heart’s desires;
the covetous blasphemes and spurns the Lord.
In his pride the wicked says: ‘He will not punish.
There is no God.’ Such are his thoughts.
Lord, do not forget the poor.
His mouth is full of cursing, guile, oppression,
mischief and deceit under his tongue.
He lies in wait among the reeds;
the innocent he murders in secret.
Lord, do not forget the poor.
His eyes are on the watch for the helpless man.
But you have seen the trouble and sorrow,
you note it, you take it in hand.
The helpless trusts himself to you;
for you are the helper of the orphan.
Lord, do not forget the poor.
readings.refrain: Lord, do not forget the poor.

exegesis.summary: The psalmist cries out to a God who seems to hide while the poor are hunted like prey by the proud. Yet the prayer is not despair but confidence: God has seen, God has noted, God will take the cause of the helpless into His own hand. The refrain, 'Lord, do not forget the poor,' is at once a plea and a profession that He never does.

patristicQuotes.quote: His barns bursting from the abundance of his stores, yet was his greedy mind by no means satisfied... His mind is distressed on account of his fruits, lest perchance when they have come forth they should profit the poor; like the glutton who had rather burst from eating, than give any thing of what remains to the starving.

He lay at his gate for this reason, that the rich might not say, I never saw him... Thou seest the death of thy body lying before the gate, and thou pitiest not. What thou throwest away from thy table, afford for alms, make thy losses gain.

exegesis.thematicConnection: The psalm answers Micah's woe: while the wicked plot in bed, the poor throw themselves upon the Lord, who is quietly preparing His answer — the humble Servant of Matthew's Gospel who will not shout in the streets but will lead justice to victory.

readings.title: Gospel
readings.text:
The Pharisees went out and began to plot against Jesus, discussing how to destroy him.
Here is my servant whom I have chosen,
my beloved, the favourite of my soul.
I will endow him with my spirit,
and he will proclaim the true faith to the nations.
He will not brawl or shout,
nor will anyone hear his voice in the streets.
He will not break the crushed reed,
nor put out the smouldering wick
till he has led the truth to victory:
in his name the nations will put their hope.

exegesis.summary: As the Pharisees withdraw to plot Jesus' destruction, He withdraws too — not to defend Himself, but to fulfill Isaiah's oracle of the chosen Servant. He will not brawl or shout, will not break the bruised reed or quench the smoldering wick, but will patiently carry justice to victory and become the hope of the nations. The Lord's response to human plotting is not violence but the meek strength of divine love, in whom Jew and Gentile alike find their rescue.

patristicQuotes.quote: The Pharisees are moved with jealousy at what had been done; because beholding the outward body of a man, they did not recognize the God in His works.

He who undertakes the office of preacher ought not to do evil, but to suffer it, and by his meekness to mollify the wrath of the angry, and by his wounds to heal the wounds of sinners in their affliction.

exegesis.thematicConnection: The Pharisees now enact what Micah condemned: they plot on their beds to destroy the innocent. But the Servant they scheme against is the very One in whom the poor of the psalm find their helper — He is the crushed reed's tenderness and the answer to 'Lord, do not forget the poor.'

synthesis.title: The Servant who does not forget the poor
synthesis.body: Today the Church sets before us two kinds of plotting. Micah unmasks the first: men who lie awake devising evil, whose hands are strong enough at dawn to seize the fields, the houses, the very inheritance of their neighbors. The Gospel shows us the same conspiracy grown to its fullness — the Pharisees withdrawing to plan how they might destroy Jesus Himself. Between these two scenes stands the Psalm, the prayer of every crushed reed and every smoldering wick: 'Lord, why do you stand afar off? Lord, do not forget the poor.' The answer is Christ. He is the chosen Servant who will not shout or brawl in the streets, who will not snap the bruised reed the oppressors have left behind, but will carry justice quietly to victory and become the hope of the nations. As the Fathers teach us, we possess nothing as lords, only as stewards; what we hoard becomes rust, what we share becomes Christ Himself received in the poor (CCC 2445, 2449). To follow this meek Servant is to renounce every scheme of the covetous heart and to become, with Him, one who remembers the poor because God has never forgotten them — or us.
